paras: The whipping of the Bellamy family was a night attack in Kentucky in March 1881, in which a masked party of self-styled regulators whipped a man named Bellamy, his three sons and two neighborhood women "for alleged immorality." The raiders also threatened to hang Bellamy's son-in-law, John Snider, who escaped and went into hiding. Papers reported it as part of a regulator "reign of terror" around Grayson.

A dispatch from Grayson described bands of men "styling themselves Regulators" committing "unlawful depredations" in Grayson's county and in the adjoining county of Greenup. The same dispatch gave most of its space to a separate conflict at Hunnewell Furnace in Greenup County, where regulators had ordered the superintendent and his son to leave after they hired about forty Black ore-diggers from Virginia. The dispatch did not connect that conflict to the Bellamy whipping.

"One night last week," according to the dispatch, a party of regulators went to Bellamy's house on the Smoky Fork of the Buffalo Fork of Tygart, "in this county." They called out "old man Bellamy" and his three sons and gave each of them thirty-nine lashes with hickory withes. The masked, well-armed raiders also whipped two women of the neighborhood "for the same offense."
Bellamy's son-in-law, John Snider, was threatened with hanging but escaped.

At the time of the dispatch, Snider was "lying out," afraid to return to his wife and family. Eight regulators were jailed at Catlettsburg over the furnace conflict; no arrests, charges or trial for the Bellamy whipping appear in the coverage.

The story is known from one Grayson dispatch printed by the Wheeling Register on March 31, 1881, and by the Lexington Kentucky Gazette on April 2. The Register headed it "Kentucky Regulators" and "Inaugurate a Reign of Terror in Certain Localities," while the Gazette ran it as "Rough Riders. Bad Work of Kentucky Regulators," with the deck line "The Persuasive Power of Hickory. Withes." Both condemned the regulators; the Gazette's fuller opening called the furnace raiders "irresponsible ruffians."
Neither paper gave the race of the Bellamys, the women or Snider, though both identified the furnace workers as Black.
